one_line: Divakar Kumar shows how to add an agent tier for gray-zone fraud decisions in an event-sourced system, feeding agents a semantic read layer built from CDC and broker events.
summary: The speaker argues that AI agents pay off inside business workflows, using real-time fraud decisions as the example. A rule engine and an ML model stay as tier 1, and only uncertain "gray zone" transactions escalate to an agent tier 2. The agents lack context, so the team built a semantic layer (projections or materialized views) fed by change feeds and message broker events from the transaction, account, device and payment contexts. Cross-context communication runs through a saga-style orchestrator, and two specialist agents (risk and behavior) run in fan-out, with a third agent reconciling their outputs into a verdict. Agent memory is short-term and in-memory because the transaction path must finish under 500 ms, and the reasoning loop has an explicit break condition. The talk is architecture-level with a live demo on synthetic data that was still loading, and it gives no accuracy, false-positive or latency measurements.

key_ideas.idea: Agents belong in business workflows, not only chatbots or coding assistants.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker uses real-time fraud detection as the workflow. The value comes from putting agents into a live decision path.

key_ideas.idea: Keep the existing rule and ML engines as tier 1 and escalate only gray-zone cases to agents.
key_ideas.detail: Most transactions are clear-cut and the existing engines handle them. Agents take only the uncertain middle band, so the existing system is not replaced.

key_ideas.idea: The real gap is missing context, not model choice.
key_ideas.detail: Rule and ML engines lacked real-time cross-domain data. The fix was to gather that data from several bounded contexts into one place the agent can query.

key_ideas.idea: Build a semantic layer (materialized view) from change feeds and broker events.
key_ideas.detail: Each bounded context pushes its events through CDC or the message broker into projections. A worker process reshapes them, and agent tools query the result instead of the write stores.

key_ideas.idea: Event sourcing stores business facts, and change feeds drive several read models.
key_ideas.detail: Commands are appended as events to Cosmos DB and never mutate state. The change feed feeds read models for timelines, customer info and fraud indicators.

key_ideas.idea: Use a saga-style orchestrator as the only cross-context path, with the agent inside it.
key_ideas.detail: All integration events pass through the orchestrator. Tier 1 and tier 2 are sub-orchestrators, and the agent tier sits behind the same message flow.

key_ideas.idea: Fan out to specialist agents and reconcile with a verdict agent.
key_ideas.detail: A risk analyzer and a behavior analyzer run in parallel. The speaker says a metric-based verdict repeated the rule engine's false positives, so a third agent weighs both outputs.

key_ideas.idea: Set a hard stop on agent reasoning loops and use short-term memory under a latency SLA.
key_ideas.detail: The loop breaks after a configured limit to avoid infinite loops, and the limit varies by use case. Memory is in-memory only because a transaction must finish in under 500 ms.

techniques.name: Tier-2 escalation for gray-zone cases
techniques.how: Keep the deterministic rule engine and ML scorer as the first pass. Send only cases between the approve and block thresholds to an agent layer.
techniques.when: An existing decision system is mostly right, but a known band of uncertain cases needs richer reasoning.

techniques.name: Semantic layer built from CDC and broker events
techniques.how: Each bounded context publishes integration events. A worker process reshapes them into per-domain projections, and agent tools read only those projections.
techniques.when: Agents need data from several services, but the services must not share databases and the agents must not query write stores.

techniques.name: Fan-out to specialist agents with a verdict agent
techniques.how: Send one event to parallel specialist agents, each with its own tools. A third agent reads their outputs and returns a single verdict event.
techniques.when: A decision depends on several signals that are better handled separately, such as risk history and behavior patterns.

techniques.name: Saga-style orchestrator as the sole cross-context router
techniques.how: Route every integration event through an orchestration layer. The layer forwards events to the contexts that need them and emits the final outcome to the broker.
techniques.when: Bounded contexts must stay decoupled and a multi-step workflow needs one place to track the sequence.

techniques.name: Hard cap on the agent reasoning loop
techniques.how: Set an explicit break condition (for example, an iteration or budget limit) per use case so the loop cannot run forever.
techniques.when: Any agent that loops over tool calls in a latency-sensitive or costed path.

techniques.name: In-memory short-term agent memory under an SLA
techniques.how: Keep only per-request context in memory and do not use long-term memory when the response budget is tight.
techniques.when: The decision must be returned within a strict latency target, such as 500 ms.

tools: Azure Cosmos DB (event store and change feed)

numbers.claim: Example purchase: a $3,500 laptop declined on two attempts, then a verification call (anecdote, not a metric).
Rule-based engine ran for about five years before the team moved to a third-party ML model.
Transaction processing SLA is under 500 ms, which is why memory is short-term and in-memory.
Four bounded contexts (transaction, accounts, device, payment) plus an orchestrator and a semantic layer.
Three read models in the transaction context: timelines, customer information, fraud indicators.
Tier 2 runs two parallel specialist agents (risk, behavior) plus one verdict agent.
No accuracy, false-positive rate, or latency result is reported. The demo runs on synthetic data and was still starting up on screen.

hot_takes: Agents are most valuable inside business workflows, not as chatbots or coding assistants.
A metric-based verdict over agent outputs can recreate the rule engine's false positives, so a reasoning verdict step is worth its cost.
Long-term memory is the wrong default when the transaction SLA is under 500 ms.

relevance.why: The talk's tiered escalation (cheap deterministic first, agent only for uncertain cases) and the hard loop cap map onto AgentOS's proxy-side budgets and routing ideas.
relevance.action: Prototype a tier-1/tier-2 route in the Govrix proxy: deterministic checks first, escalate only uncertain requests, with a loop or budget cap written into the manifest.

relevance.why: ProsHarness runs plan, critique and debate loops. The talk's explicit loop break condition and fan-out with a reconciling verdict step apply directly.
relevance.action: Add an explicit iteration cap and stop condition to the ProsHarness plan-critique loop, and test a verdict step that merges two parallel reviewer outputs before the next checkpoint.

relevance.why: Fits the recurring interests in multi-agent orchestration and cheap-model pipelines: a small first pass, with an LLM agent only on the uncertain slice.
relevance.action: Write a short design note for a cheap-first pipeline where a rule or small-model pass decides clear cases and only gray-zone items reach an LLM agent, with fan-out to two specialist checks.
